findings.title: Options object enables rejectOnClear by default despite the documented false default
findings.cause: When an options object is passed, line 7 destructures `rejectOnClear = true`; the public contract in readme.md and index.d.ts says the default is false.
findings.impact: Code using the documented `pLimit({concurrency: 1})` form can unexpectedly reject queued promises with AbortError when `clearQueue()` is called. Callers using `Promise.all` or attached rejection handlers see a rejection even though they did not opt into rejection-on-clear semantics.
evidence: index.js:7 sets `rejectOnClear = true` for options objects.
readme.md:46-52 and index.d.ts:99-106 document `rejectOnClear` as boolean with default false.
Focused probe output: {"pendingCount":0,"state":"rejected:AbortError"} after `pLimit({concurrency: 1})`, queueing a pending job, and calling `clearQueue()`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit({concurrency: 1}); limit(() => new Promise(() => {})); const pending = limit(() => 'pending-ran'); let state = 'pending'; pending.then(value => { state = 'fulfilled:' + value; }, error => { state = 'rejected:' + error.name; }); await Promise.resolve(); limit.clearQueue(); await Promise.resolve(); console.log(JSON.stringify({pendingCount: limit.pendingCount, state}));"

findings.title: Falsey non-boolean rejectOnClear values bypass runtime validation
findings.cause: Line 12 validates with `rejectOnClear && typeof rejectOnClear !== 'boolean'`, so falsey non-booleans such as null, 0, and empty string skip the TypeError path.
findings.impact: Invalid option values are silently accepted and treated as disabled, violating the documented boolean option contract and making configuration mistakes harder to catch.
evidence: readme.md:46-49 and index.d.ts:99-106 specify a boolean option.
Focused probe output accepted all three invalid values: {"value":null,"accepted":true}, {"value":0,"accepted":true}, {"value":"","accepted":true}.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; for (const value of [null, 0, '']) { try { pLimit({concurrency: 1, rejectOnClear: value}); console.log(JSON.stringify({value, accepted: true})); } catch (error) { console.log(JSON.stringify({value, accepted: false, error: error.message})); } }"

findings.title: limit.map drops the mapper index for non-array iterables
findings.cause: Lines 108-112 compute an index but pass it only when `Array.isArray(iterable)` is true, replacing the Array.from index with undefined for Set, generator, and iterator inputs.
findings.impact: The documented iterable support becomes inconsistent: mappers over Sets, generators, and array iterators cannot use the index even though the docs and types promise `(input, index)`. Existing tests cover Set values but do not assert the index.
evidence: readme.md:78-85 and index.d.ts:29-43 say every iterable mapper receives the item value and index and is equivalent to Array.from(..., (item, index) => ...).
Focused array-iterator probe output: [[10,null],[20,null]] after JSON serialization, meaning the runtime index argument was undefined.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; const limit = pLimit(2); const result = await limit.map(new Set(['a', 'b', 'c']), (value, index) => value + ':' + index); console.log(JSON.stringify(result));"

findings.title: limitFunction wrapper discards all call arguments
findings.cause: Line 124 returns a zero-argument wrapper and calls `function_()` without forwarding the wrapper's arguments.
findings.impact: Any limited function that depends on its parameters receives undefined values at runtime. This breaks the TypeScript signature and recipe usage where the returned function is called with input arguments.
evidence: index.d.ts:133-136 declares the returned function as `(...arguments_: Arguments) => Promise<ReturnType>`.
recipes.md:161-163 uses `limitedFetchUrl(url)`, which depends on forwarding the URL argument.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import {limitFunction} from './index.js'; const limited = limitFunction(async (a, b) => String(a) + ':' + String(b), {concurrency: 1}); console.log(await limited('left', 'right'));"

findings.title: validateConcurrency rejects Infinity, removing the unlimited-concurrency mode
findings.cause: Line 128 now requires `Number.isInteger(concurrency) && concurrency > 0`; the repo baseline allowed `concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY` as a valid positive concurrency value.
findings.impact: Consumers that use `pLimit(Infinity)` to disable limiting while preserving the same code path now receive a TypeError. This is a behavioral regression from the package's own previous validator.
evidence: Current index.js:127-130 rejects any non-integer concurrency.
git show HEAD:index.js:123-125 accepted `(Number.isInteger(concurrency) || concurrency === Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY) && concurrency > 0`.
Focused probe output: {"accepted":false,"name":"TypeError","message":"Expected `concurrency` to be a number from 1 and up"} for `pLimit(Infinity)`.
findings.reproduction_or_test: node --input-type=module -e "import pLimit from './index.js'; try { const limit = pLimit(Infinity); console.log(JSON.stringify({accepted: true, concurrency: limit.concurrency})); } catch (error) { console.log(JSON.stringify({accepted: false, name: error.name, message: error.message})); }"
